vjimc-2005-cat1-01.title: Half-angle substitution
vjimc-2005-cat1-01.body:
Every $z\in S_0$ can be written uniquely as $z=\cos t+i\sin t$ with $t\in(-\pi,\pi)$ (the value $t=\pi$ corresponds to $z=-1$, which is excluded). By the half-angle formulas
$$f(z)=\frac{\sin t}{1+\cos t}=\frac{2\sin\frac t2\cos\frac t2}{2\cos^2\frac t2}=\tan\frac t2 .$$
The map $t\mapsto t/2$ is a bijection $(-\pi,\pi)\to(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2)$ and $\tan$ is a bijection $(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2)\to\mathbb R$; composing with the bijection $t\mapsto e^{it}$ from $(-\pi,\pi)$ onto $S_0$ shows that $f\colon S_0\to\mathbb R$ is a bijection.

**Inverse.** If $y=\tan\frac t2$, then $z=e^{it}=e^{2i\arctan y}$. Since $1+iy$ has argument $\arctan y$ and modulus $\sqrt{1+y^2}$,
$$f^{-1}(y)=\frac{(1+iy)^2}{1+y^2}=\frac{1+iy}{1-iy}=\frac{1-y^2}{1+y^2}+\frac{2y}{1+y^2}\,i .$$
(Equivalently $t=\pm\arccos\frac{1-y^2}{1+y^2}$ with the sign of $y$.) ∎

vjimc-2005-cat1-01.title: Solve for $z$ directly
vjimc-2005-cat1-01.body:
Fix $y\in\mathbb R$ and look for $z=u+iv\in S_0$ with $f(z)=y$, i.e. $v=y(1+u)$, $u^2+v^2=1$, $u\ne-1$. Substituting,
$$1-u^2=y^2(1+u)^2\iff(1+u)(1-u)=y^2(1+u)^2\iff 1-u=y^2(1+u)$$
(we may divide by $1+u\ne0$). Hence $u=\dfrac{1-y^2}{1+y^2}$, which is $\ne-1$, and $v=y(1+u)=\dfrac{2y}{1+y^2}$. Conversely this point satisfies $u^2+v^2=\frac{(1-y^2)^2+4y^2}{(1+y^2)^2}=1$, so it lies in $S_0$ and $f(u+iv)=y$.

Thus for each $y$ there is **exactly one** $z\in S_0$ with $f(z)=y$, i.e. $f$ is a bijection, and
$$f^{-1}(y)=\frac{1-y^2}{1+y^2}+i\,\frac{2y}{1+y^2}=\frac{1+iy}{1-iy}. \qquad ∎$$

vjimc-2005-cat1-02.title: Transposing $3\times3$ arrays
vjimc-2005-cat1-02.body:
Condition (b) says: if we arrange nine elements in a $3\times3$ array, applying $f$ to the rows and then to the results gives the same as applying $f$ to the columns and then to the results. By (a), $f(a,a,a)=a$, $f(x,a,a)=x$ and $f(a,a,x)=x$; these let us rewrite any element as a row of an array.

**Neutral element $a$.** $a+x=f(a,a,x)=x$ and $x+a=f(x,a,a)=x$.

**Associativity.**
$$(x+y)+z=f\big(f(x,a,y),\,a,\,z\big)=f\big(f(x,a,y),\,f(a,a,a),\,f(a,a,z)\big).$$
The rows are $(x,a,y),(a,a,a),(a,a,z)$; the columns are $(x,a,a),(a,a,a),(y,a,z)$. By (b),
$$(x+y)+z=f\big(f(x,a,a),f(a,a,a),f(y,a,z)\big)=f\big(x,a,f(y,a,z)\big)=x+(y+z).$$

**Commutativity.** Using rows $(a,a,x),(a,a,a),(y,a,a)$, whose columns are $(a,a,y),(a,a,a),(x,a,a)$:
$$x+y=f(x,a,y)=f\big(f(a,a,x),f(a,a,a),f(y,a,a)\big)=f\big(f(a,a,y),f(a,a,a),f(x,a,a)\big)=f(y,a,x)=y+x.$$

**Inverses.** Put $-x=f(a,x,a)$. Using rows $(x,a,a),(a,a,a),(a,x,a)$, whose columns are $(x,a,a),(a,a,x),(a,a,a)$:
$$x+(-x)=f\big(x,a,f(a,x,a)\big)=f\big(f(x,a,a),f(a,a,a),f(a,x,a)\big)=f\big(f(x,a,a),f(a,a,x),f(a,a,a)\big)=f(x,x,a)=a,$$
where the last step is (a). By commutativity also $(-x)+x=a$.

Hence $(A,+)$ is an abelian group with neutral element $a$. ∎

vjimc-2005-cat1-03.title: Reduce to a polynomial identity and compare leading coefficients
vjimc-2005-cat1-03.body:
**Reformulation.** Let $P$ satisfy the condition and put $S(n)=\sum_{i=1}^n P(2i-1)=\lambda nP(n)$. Subtracting consecutive values, $P(2n+1)=S(n+1)-S(n)=\lambda\big((n+1)P(n+1)-nP(n)\big)$ for all $n\ge1$. Both sides are polynomials in $n$ agreeing at infinitely many points, hence
$$P(2x+1)=\lambda\big((x+1)P(x+1)-xP(x)\big)\quad\text{as polynomials.}\tag{1}$$
Conversely, if (1) holds, then $x=0$ gives $P(1)=\lambda P(1)$, i.e. $S(1)=\lambda\cdot1\cdot P(1)$, and summing (1) for $x=1,\dots,n-1$ gives $S(n)=\lambda nP(n)$ by induction. So we must solve (1) with $P\ne0$.

**Necessary condition on $\lambda$.** Let $P(x)=ax^k+Q(x)$ with $a\ne0$, $\deg Q<k$. Then
$$(x+1)P(x+1)-xP(x)=a\big((x+1)^{k+1}-x^{k+1}\big)+\big((x+1)Q(x+1)-xQ(x)\big)=a(k+1)x^k+(\text{lower terms}),$$
while $P(2x+1)=2^kax^k+(\text{lower terms})$. Comparing the $x^k$-coefficients in (1): $2^ka=\lambda(k+1)a$, so $\lambda=\dfrac{2^k}{k+1}$.

**Sufficiency.** Let $\lambda=\frac{2^k}{k+1}$ and let $\mathcal P_k$ be the space of real polynomials of degree $\le k$ (dimension $k+1$). The linear map $T(P)=P(2x+1)-\lambda\big((x+1)P(x+1)-xP(x)\big)$ maps $\mathcal P_k$ into $\mathcal P_k$, and by the computation above the $x^k$-coefficient of $T(P)$ is $(2^k-\lambda(k+1))a=0$. So $T\colon\mathcal P_k\to\mathcal P_{k-1}$, a space of smaller dimension; hence $\ker T\ne\{0\}$ and a non-zero solution exists. (Examples: $k=0,1$: $\lambda=1$, $P=1$; $k=2$: $\lambda=\frac43$, $P=x^2-1$.)

So the admissible $\lambda$ are exactly $\frac{2^k}{k+1}$, $k=0,1,2,\dots$

**The case $\lambda=2$.** If $P\ne0$ has degree $k$, then $\frac{2^k}{k+1}=2$, i.e. $2^{k-1}=k+1$, whose only solution in non-negative integers is $k=3$ ($k\le2$ fails directly, and $2^{k-1}>k+1$ for $k\ge4$). Put $x=0$ in (1): $P(1)=2P(1)$, so $P(1)=0$. Put $x=-1$: $P(-1)=2\big(0+P(-1)\big)$, so $P(-1)=0$. Hence $P(x)=(x-1)(x+1)(cx+d)$. The original condition with $n=2$ gives $P(1)+P(3)=4P(2)$, i.e. $8(3c+d)=12(2c+d)$, so $d=0$ and $P(x)=c(x^3-x)$.

Conversely $P(x)=x^3-x$ works: $\sum_{i=1}^n\big((2i-1)^3-(2i-1)\big)=n^2(2n^2-1)-n^2=2n^2(n^2-1)=2n\,P(n)$, using $\sum_{i=1}^n(2i-1)^3=n^2(2n^2-1)$ and $\sum_{i=1}^n(2i-1)=n^2$.

**Answer:** $\lambda\in\{2^k/(k+1):k\ge0\}$; for $\lambda=2$: $P(x)=c(x^3-x)$, $c\ne0$. ∎

vjimc-2005-cat1-04.title: Bernoulli's inequality and Stolz–Cesàro
vjimc-2005-cat1-04.body:
**Positivity.** If $x_n>0$, then $1+nx_n>1$, so $x_{n+1}=\sqrt[n]{1+nx_n}-1>0$. By induction all $x_n>0$, and the recurrence is equivalent to
$$(1+x_{n+1})^n=1+nx_n .\tag{1}$$

**(a)** By the binomial theorem (all terms positive), for $n\ge2$
$$1+nx_n=(1+x_{n+1})^n\ge1+nx_{n+1}+\binom n2x_{n+1}^2,$$
so
$$x_n-x_{n+1}\ge\frac{n-1}{2}\,x_{n+1}^2>0 .\tag{2}$$
Thus $(x_n)$ is strictly decreasing and bounded below by $0$, hence convergent; let $x=\lim x_n\ge0$. Since $x_{n+1}\ge x$, (2) gives $x_n-x_{n+1}\ge\frac{n-1}2x^2$, i.e. $x^2\le\frac{2(x_n-x_{n+1})}{n-1}\to0$. Hence $x=0$:
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}x_n=0 .$$

**(b)** We use the **Stolz–Cesàro theorem** (limsup form): if $(\beta_n)$ is strictly increasing with $\beta_n\to\infty$, then $\limsup\frac{\alpha_n}{\beta_n}\le\limsup\frac{\alpha_{n+1}-\alpha_n}{\beta_{n+1}-\beta_n}$. Take $\alpha_n=n$, $\beta_n=1/x_n$ (strictly increasing to $\infty$ by (a)). Then
$$\frac{\alpha_{n+1}-\alpha_n}{\beta_{n+1}-\beta_n}=\frac{x_nx_{n+1}}{x_n-x_{n+1}}\overset{(2)}{\le}\frac{x_nx_{n+1}}{\frac{n-1}2x_{n+1}^2}=\frac{2}{n-1}\cdot\frac{x_n}{x_{n+1}} .$$
To bound $x_n/x_{n+1}$, take logarithms in (1): $n\ln(1+x_{n+1})=\ln(1+nx_n)$. Using $\frac{u}{1+u}\le\ln(1+u)\le u$ for $u\ge0$,
$$\frac{nx_n}{1+nx_n}\le\ln(1+nx_n)=n\ln(1+x_{n+1})\le nx_{n+1},\quad\text{so}\quad \frac{x_n}{x_{n+1}}\le 1+nx_n .$$
Therefore
$$0\le\limsup_{n\to\infty}nx_n\le\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{2(1+nx_n)}{n-1}=\limsup_{n\to\infty}\Big(\frac2{n-1}+\frac{2n}{n-1}x_n\Big)=0,$$
using (a). Hence
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}nx_n=0 .$$
(Numerically, starting from $x_2=1$: $nx_n\approx0.49,\ 0.041,\ 0.0040$ for $n=10,100,1000$; in fact $nx_n\sim 4/n$.)

**Answer:** (a) $0$, (b) $0$. ∎
